source.title: Tracing the complexity profiles of different linguistic phenomena through the intrinsic dimension of LLM representations
source.authors: Marco Baroni; Emily Cheng; Iria de-Dios-Flores; Francesca Franzon

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present. Some figures and tables are flattened in the web text, but the relevant qualitative findings are also described in text.
record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses representational universality and reports similar layerwise processing profiles, but does not measure whether different models induce increasingly similar distances between the same inputs, or test the other listed versions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports intrinsic-dimension profiles within models and Information Imbalance between sentence-condition representations within a model. Neither is a comparison of representational distances across independently trained models. Its discussion of universality is related, but does not make these measurements tests of the listed versions. Information Imbalance validation and pruning results are not cross-model convergence results.
record.test_reason: The study measures within-model intrinsic dimension profiles and within-model Information Imbalance between minimal-pair sentence conditions across six LLMs. It never compares representations of the same inputs across different models, so it measures no inter-model alignment, scale trend, mapping, or shared features. Similar layerwise ID profiles across models are a related but different construct. The authors' discussion of universality (Huh et al., 2024) is interpretive only.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is essentially correct. The authors conclude that ID is a useful marker of linguistic complexity. They add that it points to similar processing steps across disparate LLMs and can distinguish complexity types. They suggest the conjectured universality of representations is partly due to similar ways LLMs organize linguistic processing.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies intrinsic dimension, within-model sentence-condition Information Imbalance, and layer pruning; it does not apply the original sources’ inter-model alignment test.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported ID distinction between subordination and coordination varies with sentence length: it is strong for four clauses, weaker for three, and absent or very moderate for two. The center-embedding/right-branching ID difference also changes across layer phases, merging or reversing after the generic ID peak.

fits_no_version.finding: Six pre-trained 7–14B LLMs show a mid-layer ID peak on generic text. They also show qualitatively consistent, contrast-specific ID differences for subordination, center-embedding and ambiguity, with Qwen diverging earlier.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Independently trained LLMs share similar layerwise processing-stage profiles (ID peaks and where complexity contrasts emerge), without direct cross-model representational alignment being measured.

record.code_released: https://github.com/franfranz/syntactic_complexity_in_LLMs (datasets); the paper also identifies https://github.com/chengemily1/id-llm-abstraction and https://github.com/sissa-data-science/DADApy as code/tool sources.
record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: The paper does not measure the claim’s inter-model alignment outcome or scale/capability trends. Its experiments cover six English LLMs sized 7 to 14 billion parameters, and the authors note compute limits, the need for other languages and more naturalistic data, and the need for more phenomena. Most layerwise profile results are presented in figures rather than as exact numerical values.
record.rows_left_out: Not applicable; four rows capture the cross-model profile and complexity-pattern findings. Within-model Information Imbalance comparisons and pruning outcomes were left out because they do not measure inter-model convergence.

untested.parts: No inter-model alignment measure and no size or capability sweep. The authors explicitly defer model-size dependence to future work.
There are no vision models and no image-caption pairs.
There is no comparison across random seeds.
There are no cross-model maps, stitching or relative representations.
There is no feature or circuit comparison across models.
No cross-model convergence result is measured under varying metrics or inputs.
The completeness, plateau, or causes of inter-model alignment are not measured.

record.verdict_notes: The Information Imbalance and pruning experiments are within-model and were rightly left out. The introduction's line about systems that 'converge to similar ways to handle language' is interpretive, not a measurement of convergence. The study is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: No sweep over model size or capability and no measurement of inter-model representational alignment.
No paired image-caption representations or vision-language comparison.
No comparison across random seeds of the same architecture for shared features or subspaces.
No mapping, stitching, relative-representation, or unpaired interchangeability test across models.
No comparison of recurring interpretable features or circuits across models.
The paper uses ID and Information Imbalance for its linguistic analyses, but does not test whether measures, settings, or inputs change an inter-model convergence result.
No measurement of the completeness or plateau of inter-model alignment, or test of shared data or objectives as its cause.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-9b, Llama-3-8B, OLMo-2-13B, Mistral-7B-v0.1, Pythia-12B, and Qwen-2.5-14B (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Measured TwoNN intrinsic dimension across layers on generic 100-word sequences.

conditions.value: 50k Wikitext sequences, split into five non-overlapping partitions of 10k

rows.value: All models have a mid-layer ID peak; OLMo, Pythia, and Qwen also have a late-layer peak. The authors describe the profiles as similar across models.
rows.uncertainty: Means and standard errors across five partitions; errors described as virtually invisible in the figure.
rows.note: Aggregate result across six models. Similar ID profiles are not a measurement of pairwise representational-distance alignment.
rows.check: Partly a replication of Cheng et al. (2025) ID-peak profiles. It is similarity of per-model ID curves, not cross-model representational alignment. The subject and condition are correct.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-9b, Llama-3-8B, OLMo-2-13B, Mistral-7B-v0.1, Pythia-12B, and Qwen-2.5-14B (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Measured layerwise TwoNN intrinsic dimension for coordinated and subordinated sentences.
rows.measure: Difference in layerwise ID profiles between sentence conditions
rows.value: The paper reports a consistent pattern: after the curves initially overlap, ID is higher for subordination, typically from under or just before the generic-sequence ID peak; Qwen diverges considerably earlier.
rows.uncertainty: Means and standard errors across five partitions; exact numerical values for these profiles are not stated in the text.
rows.note: Aggregate qualitative report across the six models. This measures responses to sentence complexity, not alignment between models.
rows.check: This is a within-model contrast effect. The text also notes it is strong only for 4-clause sentences (App. C.4).

rows.subject: Gemma-2-9b, Llama-3-8B, OLMo-2-13B, Mistral-7B-v0.1, Pythia-12B, and Qwen-2.5-14B (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Measured layerwise TwoNN intrinsic dimension for center-embedded and right-branching sentences.

conditions.value: before and after the generic-sequence ID peak

rows.measure: Difference in layerwise ID profiles between sentence conditions
rows.value: After initial fluctuations, center-embedding ID is higher; after the generic ID peak the curves merge or reverse, with right-branching ID higher for 4 of 6 models.
rows.uncertainty: Means and standard errors across five partitions; exact numerical values for these profiles are not stated in the text.
rows.note: Aggregate report. The layer phase and model count are stated, but the result concerns within-model sentence-condition differences.
rows.check: This is a within-model contrast effect. It is correctly linked to no version.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-9b, Llama-3-8B, OLMo-2-13B, Mistral-7B-v0.1, Pythia-12B, and Qwen-2.5-14B (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Measured layerwise TwoNN intrinsic dimension for ambiguous and unambiguous relative-clause attachment sentences.
rows.measure: Difference in layerwise ID profiles between sentence conditions
rows.value: The paper reports a general tendency for the more complex ambiguous condition to have higher ID, but says the difference tends to be small and is not clearly delimited by the generic-ID-peak phase.
rows.uncertainty: Means and standard errors across five partitions; exact numerical values for these profiles are not stated in the text.
rows.note: Aggregate qualitative report; it does not compare representations across models.
rows.check: This is a within-model contrast effect, and the difference is small. It is correctly linked to no version.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
